articles.body: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge . What I Built DriveSignal is a desk prototype of a driver monitoring cockpit. Its virtual vehicle displays speed, hazard lights, eye signals and alert stages in one view. Reviewers can play the driving demo with the camera off, acknowledge the stronger warning to see the driver's response, or let the demo continue to a simulated roadside stop. The live SmartSpectra mode uses a participant's consented camera measurement and personal eye calibration. The dashboard plots both eye measurements over the last eight seconds and keeps the count and last trigger visible after the camera stops. Decision cards explain which signal can trigger an alert and which provides context.

articles.title: Common SEO Mistakes Developers Make in JavaScript Websites
articles.excerpt: Most JavaScript websites I audit are not broken because the developer did something wrong on purpose. They are broken because the page Google sees and the page the user sees are two different pages. A…
articles.body: Most JavaScript websites I audit are not broken because the developer did something wrong on purpose. They are broken because the page Google sees and the page the user sees are two different pages. A founder builds a site with an AI tool like Lovable, Bolt, or v0, and gets a working product in a weekend. What they usually get is a Vite React single-page app, and Google sees almost none of it. The site looks finished in the browser and is nearly empty to a crawler. This post covers the ten mistakes I see most often in JavaScript websites, the fix for each one, one trap nobody warns you about, and a five-minute test that shows you exactly what Google sees. How Google Actually Handles JavaScript Google handles JavaScript in three phases: crawl, render, then index.

articles.title: My review subagents said "waiting for the notification" and handed back. 11 of 21 did it, and the parent sat idle 12 minutes
articles.excerpt: Short version: when a subagent puts its wait in the background and ends its turn with "waiting for the notification," the parent sees that as a finished task. On November 21 I dispatched 23 UI cards i…
articles.body: Short version: when a subagent puts its wait in the background and ends its turn with "waiting for the notification," the parent sees that as a finished task. On November 21 I dispatched 23 UI cards in a data platform repo, one after another. For 21 of them I can line up the subagent's transcript with the receipt timestamp. In 11 of those, the review subagent handed back before Codex had written its receipt. The parent got a message that said "still waiting," and then it stopped too. The longest stall was 12 minutes, until I typed "how's it going?" The fix was one commit: the wait now runs in the foreground in 170-second slices and returns a special exit code when it isn't done yet, so the caller just runs it again. Some background.

articles.title: The Riemann hypothesis has a new claimed proof. How to read it
articles.excerpt: On Friday a four-page PDF appeared on the personal website of Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic. In it, he writes that working with the company's Claude model he has found a proof of the Rie…
articles.body: On Friday a four-page PDF appeared on the personal website of Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic. In it, he writes that working with the company's Claude model he has found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old problem about how prime numbers are distributed, and that the method extends to the generalized hypothesis. He also writes that the argument has been formalized in Lean, a computer language for checking proofs. There is no paper. The announcement landed one day after Anthropic's stock market debut, timing Alpöge addressed head on, telling the BBC there is "an obvious cynical view" of it "but it is false." What actually exists today is an artifact, not a result.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989.

articles.body: On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.
